Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

For a random vector $X\in\mathbb R^p$ with mean $\mu$ and covariance
$\Sigma$ as in [[def-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]], assume
$\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^4<\infty$. Its **matrix variance** is
$$\sigma_0^2:=\left\|\mathbb E\!\left[\|X-\mu\|_2^2 (X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T\right]\right\|_{\rm op}.$$
When $\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}>0$, define the intrinsic ratio
$$d:=\frac{\sigma_0^2}{\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2}.$$

The expectation is entrywise. The finite fourth moment makes every entry
integrable. This definition imposes neither Huber contamination nor sample
replacement.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

derivations.claim: In $\mathbb R^2$, let $Z$ take values $\pm\sqrt{4/3}\,e_1$ with total probability $3/4$ (each sign has probability $3/8$), and $\pm\sqrt2\,e_2$ with total probability $1/4$ (each sign has probability $1/8$). Symmetry gives $\mathbb EZ=0$, and finite support gives a finite fourth moment.
Direct summation and [F1] give $\Sigma=\mathbb E[ZZ^T]=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/2)$, hence $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=3/2$ and $\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}=1$ by [F4].

The value of $\|Z\|_2^2$ is $4/3$ on the first pair and $2$ on the second, so $$\mathbb E[\|Z\|_2^2ZZ^T] =\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac34\left(\frac43\right)^2, \frac14(2)^2\right)=\operatorname{diag}(4/3,1).$$ Its operator norm is $4/3<3/2=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}$ by [F4]. Thus the statement is false.

$$G(S):=\{A=A^T\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}:A_{ij}=0 \text{ whenever }i\notin S\text{ or }j\notin S\},$$

diagonal entries as $\Sigma$. Thus all nonzero off-diagonal entries lie in
one common coordinate block of size at most $s$; no row-sparsity condition
is implied.

$$V_S:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1,\ u_i=0\text{ for }i\notin S\}.$$
When $1\le s\le p/2$, the restricted direction set is
$$U_s:=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|=2s}}V_S.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $c\in[0,+\infty]$. Define the scalar set function $c\mu$ by three disjoint branches:

$$ (c\mu)(E):=\begin{cases}0,&c=0,\\c\,\mu(E),&0<c<+\infty,\\0,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)=0,\\+\infty,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)>0.\end{cases}$$

Thus neither the zero branch nor the infinite branch forms the undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

For measures $(\mu_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ on the same measurable space and weights $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$, their **countable weighted sum** is the pointwise set function

$$\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_k\mu_k\right)(E):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(c_k\mu_k)(E),$$

using [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. Finite weighted sums are defined by the corresponding finite partial sum, with the empty weighted sum the zero set function. The fact that all these set functions are measures is [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]].

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p > 0$. For a natural number $k \ge 1$ write
$\iota(k) = k \cdot 1_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the canonical natural, which is positive
([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and write $k^{p} := \iota(k)^{p}$ for its rational
power ([[def-rational-power]]). Then

$$\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{k^{p}} \ \text{converges} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad p > 1 .$$

In particular the harmonic series $\sum_{k \ge 1} 1/k$ diverges, at $p = 1$, and
$\sum_{k \ge 1} 1/k^{2}$ converges, at $p = 2$.

**The index range is not cosmetic.** The series starts at $k = 1$ because
$1/0^{p}$ is undefined: [[def-rational-power]] gives $0^{p} = 0$ for rational
$p > 0$, and $0$ has no inverse. Sequences here are functions on $\mathbb{N}$ and
$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-series]]), so the object named above is a series
from the starting index $1$ in the sense of [[def-series]], not a series of a
sequence on $\mathbb{N}$.

**The exponent is rational, and that is a limitation of this page.** Rational
powers of a positive base are what [[def-rational-power]] supplies; real exponents
require the exponential and the logarithm, which this library develops later. The
statement above is therefore the full $p$-series theorem for every exponent this
page can name.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $P$ is a measure, and its total mass is $\zeta(6)^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-6}=1$ by [F5]. Thus [F2] makes $P$ a probability measure. The identity map is the real random variable specified by [F3], and $P(X=\pm k)=1/(2\zeta(6)k^6)$ for each $k\ge1$.

For $q=2$ and $q=4$, the truncations $Y_N=|X|^q\mathbf1_{\{|X|\le N\}}$ are nonnegative simple functions increasing to $|X|^q$. By [F4] and the finite atom masses, $$\mathbb E|X|^q=\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb E Y_N =\frac{1}{\zeta(6)}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{q-6} =\frac{\zeta(6-q)}{\zeta(6)}<\infty,$$ where convergence is [F5]. In particular $X$ is integrable by [F7], and its symmetric atom masses give $\mathbb E X=0$.

By [F6], the covariance is $\Sigma=\zeta(4)/\zeta(6)>0$, while the scalar matrix variance is $\sigma_0^2=\zeta(2)/\zeta(6)<\infty$. Therefore $$d=\frac{\sigma_0^2}{\Sigma^2} =\frac{\zeta(2)\zeta(6)}{\zeta(4)^2}$$ is finite and positive.

Fix $t>0$. The simple truncations $W_N=e^{t|X|}\mathbf1_{\{|X|\le N\}}$ increase to $e^{t|X|}$, so [F4] gives $$\mathbb E e^{t|X|} =\frac{1}{\zeta(6)}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}e^{tk}k^{-6}=+\infty.$$ Indeed the ratio of successive summands is $e^t(k/(k+1))^6\to e^t>1$, so the summands do not tend to zero and the series diverges. The law has polynomially decaying atom masses, finite matrix variance, and no finite positive exponential moment.

Input a finite sample $X_1,\ldots,X_m\in\mathbb R^p$, confidence
parameter $\beta>1$, and positive finite scale bounds
$0<\sigma_{\min}\le\sigma_{\max}$. The computational domain requires
$k=\lfloor3.5\beta\rfloor+1\le m/2$. Statistical guarantees are stated
separately: for a clean iid finite-fourth-moment law, use the matrix variance
of [[def-matrix-variance-of-a-random-vector]] and a bracket containing
$\sigma_0$. The statistical conditions are not needed merely to evaluate this
finite-sample procedure.

Partition the indices deterministically into $k$ nonempty blocks whose sizes differ by at
most one. Compute each block mean and call the earlier
[[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] to obtain the pilot $\widehat\mu$;
this uses the same sample and is not a sample split.

For a real symmetric matrix $A=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)Q^T$, define
$\psi(A)=Q\operatorname{diag}(\psi(\lambda_i))Q^T$, where
$\psi(x)=\operatorname{sign}(x)\min(|x|,1)$. The real spectral theorem
makes this definition independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis.
Define the finite grid and truncation thresholds
$$\sigma_j=2^j\sigma_{\min},\qquad J=\{j\in\mathbb Z:\sigma_{\min}\le\sigma_j<2\sigma_{\max}\},\qquad \theta_j=\frac1{\sigma_j}\sqrt{\frac\beta m}.$$
For every $j\in J$, form
$$\widehat\Sigma_{m,j} =\frac1{m\theta_j}\sum_{i=1}^m \psi\!\left(\theta_j(X_i-\widehat\mu)(X_i-\widehat\mu)^T\right).$$
Choose the smallest $j^*\in J$ such that
$$\|\widehat\Sigma_{m,k'}-\widehat\Sigma_{m,j^*}\|_{\rm op} \le6\sigma_{k'}\sqrt{\frac\beta m} \quad\text{for every }k'\in J,\ k'>j^*,$$
and output $\widehat\Sigma^*=\widehat\Sigma_{m,j^*}$.

This is the clean heavy-tail moment procedure. It makes no Huber
contamination or sample-replacement guarantee.

On the input domain in [[alg-adaptive-truncated-covariance-estimator]], the
adaptive truncated covariance procedure is total and Borel measurable as a
function of the sample.

derivations.claim: The grid condition is $0\le j<L_g$, so it has exactly $\lceil L_g\rceil$ elements. The first scale at or above $\sigma_0$ is $\bar j$, and $\sigma_{\bar j}<2\sigma_0\le2\sigma_{\max}$ puts it in the grid. Thus exactly $N_+$ required scales are $j\ge\bar j$, with $N_+\ge1$.

On the joint fixed-scale event, for every $k>\bar j$ the triangle inequality gives $\|\widehat\Sigma_k-\widehat\Sigma_{\bar j}\|\le3(\sigma_k+\sigma_{\bar j})\sqrt{\beta/m}\le6\sigma_k\sqrt{\beta/m}$. Hence $\bar j$ is admissible and the selected $j^*\le\bar j$. If they differ, the selection rule gives $\|\widehat\Sigma_{j^*}-\widehat\Sigma_{\bar j}\|\le6\sigma_{\bar j}\sqrt{\beta/m}$; if equal this distance is zero. Adding the error at $\bar j$ yields $\|\widehat\Sigma^*-\Sigma\|\le9\sigma_{\bar j}\sqrt{\beta/m}<18\sigma_0\sqrt{\beta/m}$.

A finite union bound costs at most $\sum_{j\ge\bar j}q_j$ for individual failure bounds. For a shared event $E$, the complement of $E\cap\bigcap_{j\ge\bar j}G_j$ has probability at most $\delta+hN_+e^{-\beta}$; the common failure is counted once. Applying step 2.1 proves all probability assertions.

Here $\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)$ is the diagonal matrix with the same
diagonal entries as $\Sigma$. Thus all nonzero off-diagonal entries lie in
one common coordinate block of size at most $s$; no row-sparsity condition
is implied.

$$V_S:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1,\ u_i=0\text{ for }i\notin S\}.$$

([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

derivations.claim: Suppose $s=1$ and $p\ge3$. For $1\le j\le p$, let $\Sigma_j=(M/2)I+h e_je_j^T$, where $h=\gamma M\sqrt{\log p/n}$. These matrices are diagonal, so [F1] places them in $\mathcal F_{p,1}(M)$. Since $\log p/n\le c_1$, choose $\gamma\sqrt{c_1}\le1/2$ so their largest eigenvalue is at most $M$. Their pairwise operator distance is $h$. Relative to $Q_0=N_p(0,(M/2)I)$, [F2] and $t=2h/M\le1$ give $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_j)\|Q_0)=\frac12[t-\log(1+t)]\le t^2/4.$$ The inequality follows by integrating $x/(1+x)\le x$ from $0$ to $t$. By [F3], each $n$-sample KL is at most $\gamma^2\log p$.

The remaining case with $s=1$ is $p=2$. Let $\Sigma_0=(M/2)I$ and $\Sigma_1=(M/2)I+h e_1e_1^T$, where $h=\gamma M\sqrt{\log(2e)/n}$. The sample-size condition and small $\gamma$ make both matrices members of $\mathcal F_{2,1}(M)$. With $t=2h/M\le1/2$, [F2] gives $$D(N_2(0,\Sigma_0)\|N_2(0,\Sigma_1)) =\frac12[\log(1+t)+(1+t)^{-1}-1]\le t^2/4.$$ The derivative of the bracket is $t/(1+t)^2\le t$, proving the inequality. By [F3], choose $\gamma$ small enough that the $n$-sample KL is at most $1/2$. Pinsker [F5] gives total variation at most $1/2$; [F6] then gives maximum binary testing error at least $1/16$. A wrong nearest covariance decision forces error at least $h/2$, and its decision cells are Borel by finite distance comparisons, so [F7] gives an admissible test kernel. Thus one law has probability at least $1/16$ of squared error at least $h^2/4=\gamma^2M^2\log(2e)/(4n)$, which is the required rate.

Suppose $s\ge2$, and put $k=s-1$ and $m=\lfloor(p-1)/k\rfloor$. Since $p\ge2s$, $m\ge2$. Partition $km$ of the $p-1$ coordinates other than coordinate $1$ into $k$ disjoint groups of size $m$. For each word $\omega\in[m]^k$, select its indexed coordinate in every group and form the unit vector $v_\omega\in\mathbb R^p$ with value $k^{-1/2}$ on those $k$ coordinates and zero elsewhere. There are $m^k$ words. Greedily retain a word and delete its Hamming ball of radius $\lfloor k/100\rfloor$. Each ball has at most $$\sum_{j\le k/100}\binom{k}{j}(m-1)^j \le\exp\!\left(kh(1/100)+(k/100)\log m\right)$$ words. To obtain the binomial sum bound, put $\alpha=1/100$; in $1=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}\alpha^j(1-\alpha)^{k-j}$, each weight for $j\le\alpha k$ is at least $e^{-kh(\alpha)}$, and $(m-1)^j\le m^{\alpha k}$.

Use the $p$ diagonal matrices from step 1.1 as the packing and $Q_0^{\otimes n}$ as reference. Choose $\gamma$ so their average KL is at most $\frac{1}{10}\log p$. The Fano factor $1-\frac{1}{10}-\log2/\log p>1/4$ for $p\ge3$, so [F4] gives classification error greater than $1/16$. Classify an estimator by its nearest covariance, resolving ties by least index. This rule is Borel because its decision cells are finite intersections of strict or weak comparisons of continuous distances, and [F7] turns it into a deterministic test kernel. If it is misclassified, the triangle inequality forces operator error at least $h/2$. Thus the supremum tail probability is greater than $1/16$ at threshold $h^2/4$. Because $\log(ep)=1+\log p\le2\log p$, $h^2/4\ge\gamma^2M^2\log(ep)/(8n)$, giving the required rate after reducing $c_M$ if needed.

The retained code $\mathcal W$ has pairwise Hamming distance greater than $k/100$ and $$\log|\mathcal W|\ge k[(99/100)\log m-h(1/100)] \ge\frac{9}{10}k\log m\ge\frac{9}{80}s\log(ep/s).$$ Here $h(1/100)<\frac{3}{50}$ and $\log m\ge\log2>\frac{69}{100}$. Also $m\ge p/(2s)$ because $(p-1)/(s-1)\ge p/s$ and $\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x/2$ for $x\ge2$. Thus $\log(ep/s)=1+\log(p/s)\le1+\log2+\log m\le4\log m$, and $k\ge s/2$. Further $|\mathcal W|\ge3$: if $k=1$, then $m\ge3$ and no word is removed by a radius-zero ball; if $k\ge2$, the displayed bound gives $\log|\mathcal W|\ge\frac{9}{5}\log2>\log3$. Distinct code vectors satisfy $\|v_\omega-v_{\omega'}\|_2^2=2d_H(\omega,\omega')/k>1/50$.

Define $\Sigma_\omega=(M/2)I+a(e_1v_\omega^T+v_\omega e_1^T)$, where $a=\gamma M\sqrt{s\log(ep/s)/n}$. The off-diagonal entries lie in the block formed by coordinate $1$ and the $k=s-1$ selected coordinates, so $\Sigma_\omega\in\mathcal F_{p,s}(M)$ by [F1]. The perturbation has eigenvalues $a,-a$ on $\operatorname{span}\{e_1,v_\omega\}$ and zero on its orthogonal complement. Choose $\gamma\sqrt{c_1}\le1/4$, so $a\le M/4$; then every $\Sigma_\omega$ is positive definite and has top eigenvalue at most $M$. For distinct codewords, $$\|\Sigma_\omega-\Sigma_{\omega'}\|_{\rm op} =a\|v_\omega-v_{\omega'}\|_2>a/8.$$

Let $Q_0=N_p(0,(M/2)I)$. The relative perturbation has eigenvalues $2a/M,-2a/M$ and zero otherwise. By [F2], $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_\omega)\|Q_0) =-\frac12\log(1-(2a/M)^2)\le4(a/M)^2.$$ The scalar inequality follows by integrating $(1-x)^{-1}\le2$ from $0$ to $x=(2a/M)^2\le1/2$. By [F3], the $n$-sample KL to $Q_0^{\otimes n}$ is at most $4\gamma^2s\log(ep/s)$. Since $\log|\mathcal W|\ge\frac{9}{10}s\log(ep/s)/8$, choose $\gamma^2\le\frac{9}{3200}$ so this KL is at most $\frac{1}{10}\log|\mathcal W|$.

The Fano factor obeys $$1-\frac{1}{10}-\frac{\log2}{\log|\mathcal W|} \ge1-\frac{1}{10}-\frac{\log2}{\log3}>\frac14.$$ Thus [F4] gives every classifier error greater than $1/16$. Nearest-covariance classification from any estimator is wrong only when its operator error is at least half the separation from step 3.1, hence at least $a/16$. The finite nearest-code rule is Borel by finite distance comparisons, so [F7] makes it a classifier kernel. The supremum tail probability at threshold $a^2/256$ is therefore greater than $1/16$, proving the rate for $s\ge2$.

Choose $c_1\le1/16$ and $c_M\le\gamma^2M^2/256$. The bounds from steps 2.1, 1.2, and 5.1 cover the cases $s=1,p\ge3$, $s=1,p=2$, and $s\ge2$, respectively, and give probability at least $c_1$ at threshold $c_Ms\log(ep/s)/n$. Taking the infimum over estimators and combining the cases proves the claim.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: First suppose $p\ge16$. Put $N_0=p(p-1)/2$ and let $W$ range over symmetric sign matrices with zero diagonal and independent $\{-1,1\}$ entries above the diagonal. For fixed unit $v$, $v^TWv=2\sum_{i<j}W_{ij}v_iv_j$. For $t\ge0$, put $h(t)=t-\tanh t$ and $g(t)=t^2/2-\log(\cosh t)$. By [F9], $h(0)=0$ and $h'(t)=1-\operatorname{sech}^2t=\tanh^2t\ge0$, so the mean value theorem gives $h(t)\ge0$; then $g(0)=0$ and $g'(t)=h(t)\ge0$. Evenness gives $g(t)\ge0$ for all real $t$, so $\cosh t\le e^{t^2/2}$. Since each $W_{ij}$ is a uniform sign and the signs are independent, $\mathbb E e^{\lambda v^TWv}=\prod_{i<j}\mathbb E e^{2\lambda v_iv_jW_{ij}}=\prod_{i<j}\cosh(2\lambda v_iv_j) \le\exp\!\left(2\lambda^2\sum_{i<j}v_i^2v_j^2\right)\le e^{\lambda^2}.$ Chernoff's inequality applied to both signs gives $\Pr(|v^TWv|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/4}$. By [F2], use a $1/4$-net with at most $9^p$ points; approximating each unit vector changes its quadratic form by at most $\frac12\|W\|_{\rm op}$. Thus $\|W\|_{\rm op}\le2\max_{v\text{ in net}}|v^TWv|$. A union bound at $t=8\sqrt p$ gives failure probability at most $2\cdot9^pe^{-16p}<1/2$. At least half of the sign matrices therefore satisfy $\|W\|_{\rm op}\le16\sqrt p$.

In the finite Hamming cube of upper-triangular signs, greedily retain a good matrix and delete all good matrices within Hamming distance $\lfloor N_0/8\rfloor$. Each deleted ball contains at most $\sum_{j\le N_0/8}\binom{N_0}{j}\le e^{N_0h(1/8)}$ words, where $h(t)=-t\log t-(1-t)\log(1-t)$. For $\alpha=1/8$, the binomial theorem gives $1=\sum_{j=0}^{N_0}\binom{N_0}{j}\alpha^j(1-\alpha)^{N_0-j}$. Each weight with $j\le\alpha N_0$ is at least $\alpha^{\alpha N_0}(1-\alpha)^{(1-\alpha)N_0}=e^{-N_0h(\alpha)}$, which proves the ball bound. Greedy deletion retains at least $2^{N_0-1}e^{-N_0h(1/8)}$ words. The resulting code $\mathcal W$ has pairwise Hamming distance greater than $N_0/8$ and $$\log|\mathcal W|\ge N_0(\log2-h(1/8))-\log2 \ge\frac1{20}p^2.$$ Here $h(1/8)<\frac{19}{50}$, $N_0\ge p^2/3$, and $p\ge16$. For distinct code matrices, $\|W-W'\|_F^2$ is eight times their upper-triangular Hamming distance, hence at least $N_0$.

Now suppose $1\le p\le15$. Set $\Sigma_0=(M/2)I$ and $\Sigma_1=(M/2)I+h e_1e_1^T$, where $h=\gamma M\sqrt{p/n}$. The condition $p/n\le c_1$ and small $\gamma$ make both matrices members of $\mathcal F_p(M)$. With $t=2h/M\le1/2$, [F3] gives $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_0)\|N_p(0,\Sigma_1)) =\frac12[\log(1+t)+(1+t)^{-1}-1]\le t^2/4.$$ The derivative of the bracket is $t/(1+t)^2\le t$, proving the bound. By [F4], the $n$-sample KL is at most $\gamma^2p\le15\gamma^2$; choose $\gamma$ so it is at most $1/2$.

Set $\Sigma_W=(M/2)I+(a/\sqrt p)W$ with $a=\gamma M\sqrt{p/n}$, where $\gamma>0$ is sufficiently small. Since $\|W\|_{\rm op}\le16\sqrt p$, the perturbation has norm at most $16a$; choose $\gamma\sqrt{c_1}\le1/64$ so $16a\le M/4$. Thus each $\Sigma_W$ is positive definite and belongs to $\mathcal F_p(M)$ by [F1]. If $W\ne W'$, [F8] gives $$\|\Sigma_W-\Sigma_{W'}\|_{\rm op} \ge\frac ap\|W-W'\|_F \ge a\sqrt{\frac{N_0}{p^2}}\ge\frac a2.$$

Pinsker [F6] gives $\|P_0^{\otimes n}-P_1^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\le1/2$. By [F7], every binary test has maximum error probability at least $1/16$. The nearest-covariance test from an arbitrary estimator is wrong only when its operator error is at least $h/2$; its two decision cells are Borel by finite distance comparisons, so [F10] makes it an admissible test kernel. Therefore one of the two laws has probability at least $1/16$ of squared error at least $h^2/4=\gamma^2M^2p/(4n)$. This proves the rate for $p\le15$.

Let $Q_0=N_p(0,(M/2)I)$ be a reference law. For each $W$, the relative perturbation has eigenvalues $r_i$ with $|r_i|\le1/2$ and $\sum_i r_i=0$. By [F3], $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_W)\|Q_0) =\frac12\sum_i(r_i-\log(1+r_i)) \le\frac12\sum_i r_i^2\le2(a/M)^2p.$$ The scalar inequality follows by integrating $t/(1+t)$ from zero to $r_i$ and using $|t/(1+t)|\le2|t|$ for $|t|\le1/2$. Also $\sum_i r_i^2=4a^2\|W\|_F^2/(M^2p)$ and $\|W\|_F^2=2N_0$. By [F4], the average $n$-sample KL to $Q_0^{\otimes n}$ is at most $2\gamma^2p^2$. Choose $\gamma$ smaller if needed so this is at most $\frac1{10}\log|\mathcal W|$.

The Fano factor in [F5] satisfies $$1-\frac1{10}-\frac{\log2}{\log|\mathcal W|}>\frac12,$$ using $\log|\mathcal W|\ge p^2/20$ and $p\ge16$. Thus every classifier of the uniform index has error probability greater than $1/8$. Classify an estimator by its nearest $\Sigma_W$, resolving ties by least index. This rule is Borel: its decision cell for index $j$ is the finite intersection of strict distance comparisons against earlier indices and weak comparisons against later indices. If it is wrong, the triangle inequality and step 2.1 force operator error at least $a/4$. Thus the supremum tail probability at threshold $a^2/16$ is greater than $1/8$. Since $a^2=\gamma^2M^2p/n$, this proves the rate for $p\ge16$.

Choose $c_1\le1/16$ and $c_M\le\gamma^2M^2/16$. Steps 4.1 and 2.2 give a probability lower bound at least $c_1$ at threshold $c_Mp/n$ in their respective dimension ranges. Taking the infimum over estimators and combining the ranges proves the first, small-ratio assertion for all dimensions satisfying its premise.

Abbreviate the constants just established by $b=c_M>0$ and $c=c_1\in(0,1/16]$, and put $a_M=\min\{bc/2,M^2c/64\}$. If $p/n\le c$, step 5.1 gives tail probability at least $c$ at threshold $bp/n$. Since $a_M\le b$ and $\min\{1,p/n\}\le p/n$, lowering the threshold gives the asserted capped bound in this case.

Suppose $p/n>c$ and $n\ge2/c$. Put $k=\lfloor cn\rfloor$, so $1\le k\le p$ and $c/2\le k/n\le c$. Let $J:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^p$ be the zero-padding coordinate isometry. For any Borel ambient matrix estimator $A$, the rule $A_k(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=J^TA(Jy_1,\ldots,Jy_n)J$ is Borel by [F11]. For any matrix $B$, including a nonsymmetric one, $\|J^TBJ\|_{\rm op}\le\|B\|_{\rm op}$: for each unit $u$, $\|J^TBJu\|_2\le\|BJu\|_2\le\|B\|_{\rm op}$ because $J$ is an isometry and $J^T$ discards coordinates. Every $\Theta\in\mathcal F_k(M)$ embeds as $J\Theta J^T\in\mathcal F_p(M)$ by [F1], and [F11] identifies its iid sample with zero-padded $N_k(0,\Theta)$ observations. Apply the small-ratio result of step 5.1 in dimension $k$ to $A_k$. Since $\|A_k-\Theta\|_{\rm op}\le\|A-J\Theta J^T\|_{\rm op}$, the ambient supremum tail probability is at least $c$ at threshold $bk/n\ge bc/2\ge a_M\min\{1,p/n\}$. This holds for every ambient Borel estimator.

Suppose $p/n>c$ and $n<2/c$. Take $\Sigma_0=(M/2)I_p$ and $\Sigma_1=\Sigma_0+h e_1e_1^T$, where $h=M\sqrt c/4$. Both are positive definite in $\mathcal F_p(M)$ and their operator separation is $h$. Put $t=2h/M=\sqrt c/2$. The scalar KL calculation from step 1.3 and [F3] gives $D(P_0\|P_1)=\frac12[\log(1+t)+(1+t)^{-1}-1]\le t^2/4=h^2/M^2$; the bracket has derivative $t/(1+t)^2\le t$ for $t\ge0$. Thus [F4] gives $D(P_0^{\otimes n}\|P_1^{\otimes n})\le nh^2/M^2<1/8$, and [F6] gives total variation at most $1/4$. Classify an arbitrary Borel estimator by the nearer of these two covariance matrices, resolving ties by the first index. This is a Borel binary test by [F10]. Apply the expected squared-risk theorem [F7] to that test with scalar targets $0,1$: its squared risks are exactly its error probabilities, so their maximum is at least $(1-\mathrm{TV})/8\ge3/32\ge c$. A wrong classification forces the original operator error to be at least $h/2$ by the triangle inequality. The ambient maximum tail probability is therefore at least $c$ at squared threshold $h^2/4=M^2c/64\ge a_M\min\{1,p/n\}$.

The three cases in steps 6.1, 7.1, and 7.2 cover every $p,n\ge1$. Each establishes the same probability constant $c=c_1$ at threshold $a_M\min\{1,p/n\}$ for every Borel matrix-valued estimator, so taking their infimum proves the all-regime assertion. The preceding small-ratio result remains unchanged.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: For each coordinate, $|X_j|\le\|X\|_2$ and $|x|\le(1+x^2)/2$ imply $\mathbb E|X_j|<\infty$, so every $\mu_j$ exists. Also $\mathbb E(X_j-\mu_j)^2<\infty$, since $(X_j-\mu_j)^2\le2X_j^2+2\mu_j^2$.

For every pair $j,k$, $2|(X_j-\mu_j)(X_k-\mu_k)|\le(X_j-\mu_j)^2+(X_k-\mu_k)^2$. Thus every covariance entry is integrable; all entries are finite and symmetry follows from commutativity of multiplication.

For $a\in\mathbb R^p$, $a^T\Sigma a=\mathbb E[(a^T(X-\mu))^2]\ge0$, so $\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite. Summing the diagonal entries gives $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_j\mathbb E(X_j-\mu_j)^2 =\mathbb E\sum_j(X_j-\mu_j)^2=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$; the sum is finite.

Let $p\ge1$, $0\le\epsilon\le1$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real positive
semidefinite $p\times p$ covariance matrix. For any Borel probability law
$Q$ on $\mathbb R^p$, define
$$P_{\epsilon,\Sigma,Q}:=(1-\epsilon)N_p(0,\Sigma)+\epsilon Q,$$
where $N_p(0,\Sigma)$ is the finite-dimensional Gaussian law from
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. A sample in this model consists of
independent observations with common law $P_{\epsilon,\Sigma,Q}$. The target
is the covariance $\Sigma$ of the uncontaminated Gaussian component, not the
covariance of the mixture.

This is the covariance specialization of the Huber model in
[[def-huber-contamination-model]]. It is distinct from a clean heavy-tail
moment model and from adversarial sample replacement.

For an experiment $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ with nonempty $\Theta$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), choose a sigma-algebra $\mathcal T$ on $\Theta$ and take $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ as the measurable action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Take the target-first loss $L:\Theta\times\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] with that action space. For $0\le\epsilon<1$, define
$$
\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)=\sup\{L(\theta_1,\theta_2):\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta,\ \|P_{\theta_1}-P_{\theta_2}\|_{TV}\le\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)\}.
$$
Set $\omega(1,\Theta)=\sup_{\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta}L(\theta_1,\theta_2)$, allowing $+\infty$. Total variation is the event-supremum convention $\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]], with no factor $1/2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space. If $0\le\epsilon<1$ and $\|P_0-P_1\|_{TV}\le\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)$, there are probability measures $Q_0,Q_1$ for which
$$
(1-\epsilon)P_0+\epsilon Q_0=(1-\epsilon)P_1+\epsilon Q_1.
$$

sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of

([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

derivations.claim: Fix any $\widehat\Sigma\in\mathscr E_n$. For each $\Sigma\in\Theta$, choosing $Q=P_\Sigma$ makes the one-observation Huber law equal to the clean law by [F1]. If $\omega\le M_0$, then $\frac1{16}(M_0\vee\omega)\le M_0$, so the robust supremum probability at the smaller threshold is at least the clean supremum probability at $M_0$. The clean premise therefore gives the claimed bound $c_0$ for this estimator. Taking the infimum preserves it.

Suppose $\omega>M_0$. By the definition of the finite supremum in [F2], there are $\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1\in\Theta$ with $\ell(\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1)>\omega/2$ and satisfying the total-variation condition there; when $\epsilon=1$ every pair is admissible. By [F3], choose contaminants $Q_0,Q_1$ whose one-observation Huber laws coincide at a law $R_1$. Their iid sample laws both equal $R_1^{\otimes n}$ by [F1] and [F4].

For every matrix action $A$, the triangle inequality gives $$\max_{i=0,1}\ell(\Sigma_i,A) \ge\frac14\ell(\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1) >\frac18\omega(\epsilon,\Theta) >\frac1{16}\bigl(M_0\vee\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)\bigr).$$ Indeed, one of the two distances from $A$ is at least half the distance between $\Sigma_0$ and $\Sigma_1$. semidefinite $p\times p$ covariance matrix. For any Borel probability law

$$P_{\epsilon,\Sigma,Q}:=(1-\epsilon)N_p(0,\Sigma)+\epsilon Q,$$

$U$ be a nonempty subset of this sphere, let $P$ be a probability law on
$\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Gamma\succeq0$. Its **matrix depth relative to
$U$** is
$$D_U(\Gamma,P):=\inf_{u\in U}\min\left\{ P((u^TX)^2\le u^T\Gamma u),P((u^TX)^2\ge u^T\Gamma u)\right\},$$
where $X$ has law $P$. Both weak inequalities include ties.

For observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, let
$P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ be their empirical law. Let $\beta>0$
be the constant of [[lem-matrix-depth-gaussian-scale-constant-exists-uniquely]].

These are the unrestricted-spectrum versions; no known spectral bound is needed to define their selectors.

For known $M>0$, the dense bounded-class depth correspondence is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_p(\beta M)} D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n).$$
For known integer $1\le s\le p/2$, the single-block sparse version is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_{p,s}(\beta M)} D_{U_s}(\Gamma,P_n),$$
where the classes and $U_s$ are defined in
[[def-bounded-spectrum-covariance-class]] and
[[def-block-sparse-covariance-class]]. A **measurable matrix-depth estimator**
is a Borel measurable selector $\widehat\Gamma$ from the applicable argmax
correspondence, with covariance output $\widehat\Sigma=\widehat\Gamma/\beta$.

belongs to the corresponding class; it makes no computational feasibility
claim.

$N_p(0,\Sigma)$ be its centered Gaussian law. If $\beta$ is the unique
positive constant satisfying $\Phi(\sqrt\beta)=3/4$, then
$$D_U(\beta\Sigma,N_p(0,\Sigma))\ge\frac12.$$
Equality holds for every direction with positive variance; when $\Sigma=0$
the depth is $1$.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ be independent random elements of $\mathbb R^p$ with
common Borel probability law $P$. Let $S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq[p]$ be
nonempty coordinate sets with $|S_j|\le s$, where $m,s\ge1$, and define
$$V_{S_j}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1,\ u_i=0\text{ for }i\notin S_j\}.$$
For $u\in V_{S_j}$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, put
$A_{u,t}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^p:|u^Tx|^2\le t\}$ and
$P_N(A):=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1\{X_i\in A\}$. There is a universal
constant $C$ such that, for every $0<\delta<1$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le j\le m}\sup_{\substack{u\in V_{S_j}\\t\in\mathbb R}}|P_N(A_{u,t})-P(A_{u,t})|\le C\left[\sqrt{\frac{s+1}{N}}+\sqrt{\frac{\log(m/\delta)}{N}}\right]\right)\ge1-\delta.$$
The same bound holds for the upper-tail sets
$\{x:|u^Tx|^2\ge t\}$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable

$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then

derivations.claim: Expand the finite product mixture law using independent contamination labels. The contaminated count $n_2$ is binomial. For a Bernoulli variable $B$ with mean $\epsilon$, the centered log-mgf $g(\lambda)=\log\mathbb E e^{\lambda(B-\epsilon)}$ satisfies $g(0)=g'(0)=0$ and $g''(\lambda)$ is a variance of a tilted Bernoulli law, hence at most $1/4$. Integrating twice gives $g(\lambda)\le\lambda^2/8$; Chernoff optimization gives $n_2/n\le\epsilon+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2n)}$ except on an event of probability $\delta$. Put $q=r+\log(m/\delta)$. Since $C_1q/n<1$ and $C_1\ge200$, the square-root term is at most $1/20$. Thus $n_2/n<1/4$ and $n_1=n-n_2>3n/4$.

Conditional on the label pattern and clean count $n_1$, the clean observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_{n_1}$ are independent with law $N_p(0,\Sigma)$. Apply [F3] with confidence $\delta$. Except on a conditional event of probability $\delta$, every clean empirical tail differs from its Gaussian probability by at most $e=C[\sqrt{(r+1)/n_1}+\sqrt{\log(m/\delta)/n_1}]$.

For fixed $\Gamma$ and $u$, each full-sample tail count lies between the corresponding clean count and that count plus $n_2$. Taking the minimum of the two tails and then the infimum over $u$ yields $$nD_U(\Gamma,P_n)\le n_1D_U(\Gamma,P_{n_1}^Y)+n_2, \qquad nD_U(\Gamma,P_n)\ge n_1D_U(\Gamma,P_{n_1}^Y).$$ Since $D_U(\widehat\Gamma,P_n)\ge D_U(\beta\Sigma,P_n)$ by the comparison premise, these inequalities imply $D_U(\widehat\Gamma,P_{n_1}^Y) \ge D_U(\beta\Sigma,P_{n_1}^Y)-n_2/n_1$.

On the deviation event in step 1.2, replacing clean empirical depth by population depth costs at most $e$ at each matrix. [F2] and the comparison in step 2.1 therefore imply $D_U(\widehat\Gamma,N_p(0,\Sigma))\ge1/2-n_2/n_1-2e$. Since $r\ge1$, $r+1\le2q$ and $\log(m/\delta)\le q$, we have $e\le C(\sqrt2+1)\sqrt{q/n_1} \le C(\sqrt2+1)\sqrt{4/(3C_1)}$. Choose $C_1$ large enough that $e\le1/24$. Step 1.1 gives $n_2/n_1\le1/3$. Retain the actual deficit $\rho:=n_2/n_1+2e\le5/12<1/2$. Also $n_1>3n/4$ and step 1.1 give $n_2/n_1\le(4/3)(\epsilon+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2n)})$, while $e\le C\sqrt{q/n}$; hence $\rho\le C(\epsilon+\sqrt{q/n})$.

Fix $u\in U$ and put $v=u^T\Sigma u$. If $v>0$, let $z=u^T\widehat\Gamma u/v\ge0$. The Gaussian tails at threshold $u^T\widehat\Gamma u$ are $2\Phi(\sqrt z)-1$ and $2-2\Phi(\sqrt z)$; their minimum is $1/2-2|\Phi(\sqrt z)-3/4|$. Step 3.1 therefore gives $|\Phi(\sqrt z)-\Phi(\sqrt\beta)|\le\rho/2$. The bound $\rho\le5/12$ places both Gaussian probabilities in the fixed compact interval $[13/24,23/24]\subset(0,1)$. On this interval [F4] gives $|\sqrt z-\sqrt\beta|\le C\rho$ and then $|z-\beta|\le C\rho$. Since $u^T(\widehat\Gamma/\beta-\Sigma)u=(v/\beta)(z-\beta)$ and $v\le M$, this implies $|u^T(\widehat\Gamma/\beta-\Sigma)u|\le C_M\rho\le C_M(\epsilon+\sqrt{q/n})$.

If $v=0$, [F5] gives $u^TX=0$ almost surely. If $u^T\widehat\Gamma u>0$, the upper weak tail is zero, contradicting the positive depth lower bound in step 3.1. Hence $u^T\widehat\Gamma u=0$ and the quadratic error is zero. Taking the supremum over $U$ is a Borel function of the Borel selector by [F6, F7]; its Lipschitz bound follows by applying the operator-norm inequality to the difference of two candidate matrices. Intersecting the events from steps 1.1–1.2 gives probability at least $1-2\delta$ and the stated bound.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

For $p\ge1$, write $S^{p-1}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1\}$. Let
$U$ be a nonempty subset of this sphere, let $P$ be a probability law on
$\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Gamma\succeq0$. Its **matrix depth relative to
$U$** is
$$D_U(\Gamma,P):=\inf_{u\in U}\min\left\{ P((u^TX)^2\le u^T\Gamma u),P((u^TX)^2\ge u^T\Gamma u)\right\},$$
where $X$ has law $P$. Both weak inequalities include ties.

For observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, let
$P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ be their empirical law. Let $\beta>0$
be the constant of [[lem-matrix-depth-gaussian-scale-constant-exists-uniquely]].
The **global dense** depth correspondence is $\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\succeq0}D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n)$, over symmetric positive semidefinite matrices. For $1\le s\le p/2$, define the global single-block class $\mathcal F_{p,s}:=\bigcup_{c>0}\mathcal F_{p,s}(c)$ and the **global single-block sparse** correspondence $\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_{p,s}}D_{U_s}(\Gamma,P_n)$. These are the unrestricted-spectrum versions; no known spectral bound is needed to define their selectors.

For known $M>0$, the dense bounded-class depth correspondence is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_p(\beta M)} D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n).$$
For known integer $1\le s\le p/2$, the single-block sparse version is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_{p,s}(\beta M)} D_{U_s}(\Gamma,P_n),$$
where the classes and $U_s$ are defined in
[[def-bounded-spectrum-covariance-class]] and
[[def-block-sparse-covariance-class]]. A **measurable matrix-depth estimator**
is a Borel measurable selector $\widehat\Gamma$ from the applicable argmax
correspondence, with covariance output $\widehat\Sigma=\widehat\Gamma/\beta$.
Either global correspondence or the applicable bounded-class correspondence may be used. The compact search restriction contains $\beta\Sigma$ whenever the target
belongs to the corresponding class; it makes no computational feasibility
claim.

For $M>0$ and $p\ge1$, define
$$\mathcal F_p(M):=\{\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}: \Sigma=\Sigma^T,\ \Sigma\succeq0,\ \|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}\le M\}.$$
For positive semidefinite $\Sigma$, the operator norm is its largest
eigenvalue, so this is the bounded-spectrum covariance class.

For $S\subseteq[p]$, let
$$G(S):=\{A=A^T\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}:A_{ij}=0 \text{ whenever }i\notin S\text{ or }j\notin S\},$$
and, for an integer $1\le s\le p$, let
$$G(s):=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|\le s}}G(S),\qquad \mathcal F_{p,s}(M):=\{\Sigma\in\mathcal F_p(M): \Sigma-\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)\in G(s)\}.$$
Here $\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)$ is the diagonal matrix with the same
diagonal entries as $\Sigma$. Thus all nonzero off-diagonal entries lie in
one common coordinate block of size at most $s$; no row-sparsity condition
is implied.

For $S\subseteq[p]$, define
$$V_S:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1,\ u_i=0\text{ for }i\notin S\}.$$
When $1\le s\le p/2$, the restricted direction set is
$$U_s:=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|=2s}}V_S.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $T$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$f:T\to\mathbb R$.  The map $f$ is **upper semicontinuous** if, for every
$a\in\mathbb R$, the strict sublevel set

$$\{x\in T:f(x)<a\}$$

is open in $T$.  Equivalently, every superlevel set
$\{x\in T:f(x)\geq a\}$ is closed, because it is the complement of the
strict sublevel set.

When $T=A\subseteq\mathbb R$ has the subspace topology, this agrees with the
existing pointwise definition: the equivalence with openness of all strict
sublevels is exactly [[thm-semicontinuity-level-set-characterisation]], claim
1.  The empty-domain condition is vacuous, constant functions are upper
semicontinuous, and the inequalities deliberately distinguish the open
threshold $f<a$ from the closed threshold $f\geq a$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Identify the symmetric matrices with their coordinates in $\mathbb R^{p^2}$. The dense class $K=\mathcal F_p(\beta M)$ is bounded because each entry satisfies $|\Gamma_{ij}|=|e_i^T\Gamma e_j|\le\|\Gamma\|_{\rm op}\le\beta M$ by [F3]. It is closed: if $\Gamma_k\to\Gamma$ coordinatewise with $\Gamma_k\in K$, then $\Gamma$ is symmetric, $v^T\Gamma v=\lim_k v^T\Gamma_kv\ge0$ for every $v$, and $\|\Gamma v\|_2=\lim_k\|\Gamma_kv\|_2\le\beta M\|v\|_2$ for every $v$. By the operator-norm definition in [F2], this gives $\|\Gamma\|_{\rm op}\le\beta M$. Thus $K$ is closed and bounded, so [F3] makes it compact.

Fix $u$ and write $q(\Gamma)=u^T\Gamma u$ and $r_i=(u^Tx_i)^2$. If $\Gamma_k\to\Gamma$, then $q(\Gamma_k)\to q(\Gamma)$. For each $i$, if $r_i<q(\Gamma)$ or $r_i>q(\Gamma)$, the two weak-tail indicators eventually keep their limiting membership; if $r_i=q(\Gamma)$, the observation is counted in both weak tails at $\Gamma$. Therefore the limsup of each finite tail count is at most its value at $\Gamma$, and the limsup of their minimum is at most the minimum of their values there. The minimum of the two empirical tails is upper semicontinuous in $\Gamma$. The infimum over $u$ remains upper semicontinuous because each strict sublevel set of the infimum is the union of the corresponding open strict sublevel sets from [F4]. Hence $\Gamma\mapsto D_U(\Gamma,P_n)$ is upper semicontinuous on either search class.

For each fixed $S\subseteq[p]$ with $|S|\le s$, requiring the off-diagonal entries outside $S\times S$ to vanish is a finite collection of closed coordinate equalities. Its intersection with the dense compact class is compact by [F5]. There are finitely many such $S$, and their union is $\mathcal F_{p,s}(\beta M)$ by [F2]. A finite union of compact sets is compact, since any open cover has a finite subcover on each of its finitely many members.

Both applicable search classes are nonempty because they contain the zero matrix. By steps 1.1–1.2 they are compact Euclidean sets. By step 1.2, their empirical depth functions are upper semicontinuous, so [F5] gives a maximizer on each applicable class. Its argmax is the nonempty weak superlevel set at that maximum, closed by [F4] and compact by [F5]. This proves the claim.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

For a random vector $X\in\mathbb R^p$ with mean $\mu$ and covariance
$\Sigma$ as in [[def-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]], assume
$\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^4<\infty$. Its **matrix variance** is
$$\sigma_0^2:=\left\|\mathbb E\!\left[\|X-\mu\|_2^2 (X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T\right]\right\|_{\rm op}.$$
When $\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}>0$, define the intrinsic ratio
$$d:=\frac{\sigma_0^2}{\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2}.$$

The expectation is entrywise. The finite fourth moment makes every entry
integrable. This definition imposes neither Huber contamination nor sample
replacement.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

derivations.claim: Put $Y=X-\mu$ and choose a unit top eigenvector $v$ of $\Sigma$, with $\lambda=v^T\Sigma v=\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}>0$ by [F1] and [F3]. The positive semidefinite matrix inside [F2] has operator norm at least its quadratic form at $v$, so $$\sigma_0^2\ge\mathbb E[\|Y\|_2^2(v^TY)^2] \ge\mathbb E[(v^TY)^4].$$ The second inequality follows pointwise from $\|Y\|_2^2\ge(v^TY)^2$.

The finite fourth moment makes $W=v^TY$ square-integrable. By [F4], $\mathbb E[W^4]\ge(\mathbb E[W^2])^2=\lambda^2$. Hence $\sigma_0^2\ge\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}^2$, and division by this positive quantity proves $d\ge1$.
