Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For fixed $S$, normalized nonzero rational vectors supported in $S$ are countable and dense in $V_S$: approximate the coordinates of a unit vector by rationals and normalize. For each fixed $u\in V_S$ and $t\ge0$, choose such $u_k$ with $\|u_k-u\|_2\le k^{-2}$ and rational $t_k\in(t+1/k,t+2/k)$. For fixed $x$, $$|(u_k^Tx)^2-(u^Tx)^2|\le2\|x\|_2^2k^{-2}.$$ Therefore $\mathbf1_{A_{u_k,t_k}}(x)\to\mathbf1_{A_{u,t}}(x)$, including boundary points, and [F3] gives convergence of their $P$-probabilities. The finite empirical probabilities converge pointwise too. For $t<0$ the set is empty and is represented by rational negative thresholds. Thus the supremum equals the supremum over a countable subclass and is measurable.

Fix a support $S$ of size $k\le s$. Trace patterns of affine halfspaces on $r$ fixed points are sign patterns of $r$ affine hyperplanes in a $(k+1)$-dimensional parameter space. The number of open regions is at most $\sum_{\ell=0}^{k+1}\binom r\ell$: adding one hyperplane creates at most the number of regions cut on that hyperplane, so induction on $r$ and the dimension gives Pascal's recurrence and this sum. Weak-boundary traces are also counted, since on a finite point set a halfspace threshold can be increased slightly without changing its trace.

A slab $A_{u,t}$ with $t\ge0$ is the intersection of the halfspaces $u^Tx\le\sqrt t$ and $-u^Tx\le\sqrt t$ in the same $k$ coordinates; when $t<0$ it is empty. Hence its trace count on $r$ points is at most $(\sum_{\ell=0}^{k+1}\binom r\ell)^2$. For $r\ge q:=k+1$, set $x=q/r$. Since $x^\ell\ge x^q$ for $\ell\le q$, $$\sum_{\ell=0}^q\binom r\ell\le x^{-q}(1+x)^r\le(er/q)^q.$$ If $r\ge16q$, then $2^r>(er/q)^{2q}$: the logarithmic difference is positive at $r/q=16$ and has positive derivative thereafter. Thus $r$ points cannot be shattered by the slab class, so its VC dimension is at most $16(k+1)\le16(s+1)$.

Let $\varepsilon_i$ be independent uniform signs, independent of the sample, and let $X'_1,\ldots,X'_N$ be an independent copy. Jensen's inequality [F5], conditional on the original sample, gives $$\mathbb E\sup_A|P_N(A)-P(A)| \le\mathbb E\sup_A|P_N(A)-P'_N(A)|.$$ Each pair $(X_i,X'_i)$ is exchangeable, so independently swapping its coordinates with sign $\varepsilon_i$ leaves the joint law unchanged. The triangle inequality then gives $$\mathbb E\sup_A|P_N(A)-P(A)| \le2\,\mathbb E\sup_A\left|N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\varepsilon_i\mathbf1_A(X_i)\right|.$$ The ghost sample and signs exist on finite product spaces by [F6]; all suprema use the countable class from step 1.1.

Replacing one observation changes every empirical set probability by at most $1/N$, so the supremum $F$ changes by at most $1/N$. In the Doob martingale of $F$, each conditional increment therefore has a range of width at most $1/N$. If a random variable lies in an interval of width $c$, the log-mgf of its centered version has second derivative equal to a tilted variance at most $c^2/4$; integrating twice gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)}\le e^{\lambda^2c^2/8}$. Iterating these bounds and optimizing the exponential Markov inequality yields $\mathbb P(F-\mathbb EF>t)\le e^{-2Nt^2}$.

On a fixed $N$-point sample the trace class is finite. For a fixed pair the probability that the traces agree at all sampled coordinates is at most $e^{-r\rho^2}$; a union bound over pairs shows that some coordinate sample distinguishes all $M$ traces. Writing $y=\log(M)/D$, the choice of $r$ gives $r\le C\rho^{-2}D(y+1)$ and hence $y\le2\log(C\rho^{-2}(y+1))$. Put $A=\log(C\rho^{-2})\ge1$. To obtain the sign MGF bound used for chaining, for $t\ge0$ put $h(t)=t-\tanh t$. Then $h(0)=0$ and $h'(t)=1-\operatorname{sech}^2t=\tanh^2t\ge0$ by [F8]; the mean value theorem gives $h(t)\ge0$. Its restriction to $\Theta\times\Theta$ defines the contamination modulus
$\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)$ through [[def-contamination-modulus]]. Suppose
$\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)<\infty$, $0\le M_0<\infty$, $0<c_0\le1$, and
$$\inf_{\widehat\Sigma\in\mathscr E_n}\sup_{\Sigma\in\Theta} P_\Sigma^{\otimes n}\{\ell(\Sigma,\widehat\Sigma)\ge M_0\}\ge c_0.$$
Then
$$\inf_{\widehat\Sigma\in\mathscr E_n}\sup_{\Sigma\in\Theta}\sup_Q P_{\epsilon,\Sigma,Q}^{\otimes n} \left\{\ell(\Sigma,\widehat\Sigma)\ge \frac1{16}\bigl(M_0\vee\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)\bigr)\right\} \ge\min(c_0,1/2).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

For $S\subseteq[p]$, let
$$G(S):=\{A=A^T\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}:A_{ij}=0 \text{ whenever }i\notin S\text{ or }j\notin S\},$$
and, for an integer $1\le s\le p$, let
$$G(s):=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|\le s}}G(S),\qquad \mathcal F_{p,s}(M):=\{\Sigma\in\mathcal F_p(M): \Sigma-\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)\in G(s)\}.$$
Here $\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)$ is the diagonal matrix with the same
diagonal entries as $\Sigma$. Thus all nonzero off-diagonal entries lie in
one common coordinate block of size at most $s$; no row-sparsity condition
is implied.

For $S\subseteq[p]$, define
$$V_S:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1,\ u_i=0\text{ for }i\notin S\}.$$
When $1\le s\le p/2$, the restricted direction set is
$$U_s:=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|=2s}}V_S.$$

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

Let $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le n$. Then, in $\mathbb{N}$,

$$\binom{n}{k}\cdot k!\cdot (n-k)! = n! ,$$

and consequently:

1. $\binom{n}{k}\cdot k! = n^{\underline{k}}$
   ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]);
2. **integrality**: in $\mathbb{R}$,
   $\iota\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{\iota(n!)}{\iota(k!)\,\iota((n-k)!)}$, so the
   familiar quotient $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$ is the canonical natural of a natural
   number, namely of the count $\binom{n}{k}$;
3. **symmetry**: $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$.

Here $\iota$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]] and $n-k$ the
truncated difference, which for $k \le n$ is the ordinary one.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, let $c \in \mathbb{N}$, and let
$m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with $\sum^{\mathbb{N}}$ and $\prod^{\mathbb{N}}$ as in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]] and $\sum^{\mathbb{R}}$, $\prod^{\mathbb{R}}$
as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Let $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so $\iota(0) = 0$ and
$\iota(\sigma(n)) = \iota(n) + 1$. Then:

0. **$\iota$ is additive and multiplicative.** $\iota(1) = 1$, and
   $\iota(m+n) = \iota(m) + \iota(n)$ and $\iota(m n) = \iota(m)\,\iota(n)$ for
   **all** $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, the cases where a factor is $0$ included.
1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Constants.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} c = n \cdot c$, the summand being the constant list.
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ and $d := n - m$, then
   $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{j<d} a_{m+j}$, and
   $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{j<d} a_{m+j}\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for every $k < n$ then
   $\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$; and $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every $j < n$.
5. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$;
   and if $a_k \ne 0$ for every $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ne 0$.
6. **The bridge into $\mathbb{R}$.**
   $\displaystyle\iota\Big(\sum^{\mathbb{N}}_{k<n} a_k\Big) = \sum^{\mathbb{R}}_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
   and
   $\displaystyle\iota\Big(\prod^{\mathbb{N}}_{k<n} a_k\Big) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$.
7. **$\iota$ is strictly increasing, hence injective.** $m < n$ if and only if
   $\iota(m) < \iota(n)$, and $m = n$ if and only if $\iota(m) = \iota(n)$.

Clauses 6 and 7 together are the licence used everywhere below: an identity
between natural numbers may be proved by proving the corresponding identity
between their canonical naturals in $\mathbb{R}$, and conversely a real identity
whose two sides are canonical naturals is an identity in $\mathbb{N}$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
3. If $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ then all three identities of claim 1 hold for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

For every nonempty finite sample, both the bounded-class and global dense
and block-sparse argmax correspondences in
[[def-matrix-depth-covariance-estimator]] admit Borel measurable selectors
as functions of the sample. The covariance output obtained by division by
$\beta$ is Borel as well. No computational feasibility is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F7], Borel maximizers exist in both versions and satisfy [F1]'s empirical-depth comparison. Put $k=2s$ and $m=\binom pk$. By [F8], $m\le p^k/k!$. Since $\log x\le\log j$ for $x\in[j-1,j]$ and $2\le j\le k$, summing over these intervals and using [F9] gives $\log k!=\sum_{j=2}^k\log j\ge\int_1^k\log x\,dx=k\log k-k+1\ge k\log k-k$. Exponentiating with [F9] yields $k!\ge(k/e)^k$, hence $m\le(ep/k)^k$ and $\log m\le2s\log(ep/(2s))\le2s\log(ep/s)$. Enumerate the coordinate sets of size $2s$ and take $U=U_s$, $r=2s$ in [F1]. If $A=\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma$, choose blocks of size at most $s$ supporting the off-diagonal entries of its two summands, and let $T$ be their union. Then $|T|\le2s$, entries between $T$ and $T^c$ vanish, and the block on $T^c$ is diagonal. Thus $A$ is block diagonal on $\mathbb R^T\oplus\mathbb R^{T^c}$, with symmetric block $A_T$ and diagonal block $D$ on $T^c$. Its operator norm is the larger block norm: for $x=x_T+x_{T^c}$, $\|Ax\|_2^2$ is the sum of the squared norms of the two block outputs, and a norm-maximizing vector in either nonempty finite-dimensional block attains its block norm. If $T\ne\varnothing$ and either $T^c=\varnothing$ or $\|A_T\|_{\rm op}\ge\|D\|_{\rm op}$, [F5] gives a unit eigenvector attaining $\|A_T\|_{\rm op}$, supported in $T$. In every other case $T^c\ne\varnothing$ and $\|D\|_{\rm op}>\|A_T\|_{\rm op}$ (with the empty-block norm set to zero). Write $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_i:i\in T^c)$. By [F10] choose $j\in T^c$ with $|d_j|=\max_{i\in T^c}|d_i|$. For every unit $x\in\mathbb R^{T^c}$, $|x^TDx|=|\sum_i d_ix_i^2|\le\max_i|d_i|\sum_i x_i^2=|d_j|$, and the coordinate vector $e_j$ attains equality. By [F5], $e_j$ therefore attains $\|D\|_{\rm op}$. In either case some unit vector attaining $\|A\|_{\rm op}$ has support of size at most $2s$. Since $p\ge2s$, its support extends to a set of size exactly $2s$, so the vector belongs to $U_s$. Conversely every unit vector in $U_s$ is among all unit vectors, hence $\|A\|_{\rm op}=\sup_{u\in U_s}|u^TAu|$ by [F5]. Finally, $$2s+\log(m/\delta)\le4s\log(ep/s)+\log(1/\delta) \le4\bigl(s\log(ep/s)+\log(1/\delta)\bigr).$$ Squaring [F1]'s bound proves the displayed upper rate after adjusting $C_M$.

By [F2], the clean lower premise holds at $M_0=b_Ms\log(ep/s)/n$ for sufficiently small $s\log(ep/s)/n$, with a fixed positive probability $b_0$. By [F3], the contamination modulus is at least $d_M\epsilon^2$. It is finite because $\|\Sigma_0-\Sigma_1\|_{\rm op}^2\le4M^2$ for all pairs in the bounded class.

Apply [F4] with these clean and modulus bounds and the unrestricted matrix-valued estimator class in the Statement. Its threshold $\frac1{16}(M_0\vee\omega)$ is at least a constant multiple of $s\log(ep/s)/n\vee\epsilon^2$, and the probability lower bound is $\min(b_0,1/2)$. Lowering the threshold only enlarges the event, which proves the lower assertion for the event probabilities in the Statement.

For $p\ge1$, write $S^{p-1}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1\}$. Let
$U$ be a nonempty subset of this sphere, let $P$ be a probability law on
$\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Gamma\succeq0$. Its **matrix depth relative to
$U$** is
$$D_U(\Gamma,P):=\inf_{u\in U}\min\left\{ P((u^TX)^2\le u^T\Gamma u),P((u^TX)^2\ge u^T\Gamma u)\right\},$$
where $X$ has law $P$. Both weak inequalities include ties.

For observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, let
$P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$ be their empirical law. Let $\beta>0$
be the constant of [[lem-matrix-depth-gaussian-scale-constant-exists-uniquely]].
The **global dense** depth correspondence is $\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\succeq0}D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n)$, over symmetric positive semidefinite matrices. For $1\le s\le p/2$, define the global single-block class $\mathcal F_{p,s}:=\bigcup_{c>0}\mathcal F_{p,s}(c)$ and the **global single-block sparse** correspondence $\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_{p,s}}D_{U_s}(\Gamma,P_n)$. These are the unrestricted-spectrum versions; no known spectral bound is needed to define their selectors.

For known $M>0$, the dense bounded-class depth correspondence is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_p(\beta M)} D_{S^{p-1}}(\Gamma,P_n).$$
For known integer $1\le s\le p/2$, the single-block sparse version is
$$\operatorname{Argmax}_{\Gamma\in\mathcal F_{p,s}(\beta M)} D_{U_s}(\Gamma,P_n),$$
where the classes and $U_s$ are defined in
[[def-bounded-spectrum-covariance-class]] and
[[def-block-sparse-covariance-class]]. A **measurable matrix-depth estimator**
is a Borel measurable selector $\widehat\Gamma$ from the applicable argmax
correspondence, with covariance output $\widehat\Sigma=\widehat\Gamma/\beta$.
Either global correspondence or the applicable bounded-class correspondence may be used. The compact search restriction contains $\beta\Sigma$ whenever the target
belongs to the corresponding class; it makes no computational feasibility
claim.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $T$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$f:T\to\mathbb R$.  The map $f$ is **upper semicontinuous** if, for every
$a\in\mathbb R$, the strict sublevel set

$$\{x\in T:f(x)<a\}$$

is open in $T$.  Equivalently, every superlevel set
$\{x\in T:f(x)\geq a\}$ is closed, because it is the complement of the
strict sublevel set.

When $T=A\subseteq\mathbb R$ has the subspace topology, this agrees with the
existing pointwise definition: the equivalence with openness of all strict
sublevels is exactly [[thm-semicontinuity-level-set-characterisation]], claim
1.  The empty-domain condition is vacuous, constant functions are upper
semicontinuous, and the inequalities deliberately distinguish the open
threshold $f<a$ from the closed threshold $f\geq a$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$. In the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$,
each of the following families generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$: all open
sets; all closed sets; all compact sets; all Euclidean open balls; all open
boxes; all rational open boxes; and all rational half-open boxes
$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ with rational endpoints $a_i<b_i$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For $S\subseteq[p]$, let
$$G(S):=\{A=A^T\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}:A_{ij}=0 \text{ whenever }i\notin S\text{ or }j\notin S\},$$
and, for an integer $1\le s\le p$, let
$$G(s):=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|\le s}}G(S),\qquad \mathcal F_{p,s}(M):=\{\Sigma\in\mathcal F_p(M): \Sigma-\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)\in G(s)\}.$$
Here $\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)$ is the diagonal matrix with the same
diagonal entries as $\Sigma$. Thus all nonzero off-diagonal entries lie in
one common coordinate block of size at most $s$; no row-sparsity condition
is implied.

For $S\subseteq[p]$, define
$$V_S:=\{u\in\mathbb R^p:\|u\|_2=1,\ u_i=0\text{ for }i\notin S\}.$$
When $1\le s\le p/2$, the restricted direction set is
$$U_s:=\bigcup_{\substack{S\subseteq[p]\\|S|=2s}}V_S.$$

derivations.claim: For fixed $u$, each function $(x,\Gamma)\mapsto(u^Tx_i)^2-u^T\Gamma u$ is continuous. Its nonpositive and nonnegative sets are closed, so their indicators are upper semicontinuous: outside a closed set the indicator is locally zero, and at a point of the set its limsup is at most one. Finite sums and the minimum of two upper semicontinuous maps are upper semicontinuous. The infimum over fixed $u\in U$ is also upper semicontinuous because its strict sublevel is the union of the strict sublevels for individual $u$. Thus $D$ is jointly upper semicontinuous in $(x,\Gamma)$. Every directional count minimum belongs to $\{0,1/n,\ldots,1\}$; the infimum of a nonempty subset of this finite set belongs to the same set. Ties may give depth $1$, so the full grid is retained.

Put $R(x)=\max_{i\le n}\|x_i\|_2^2$. If a positive semidefinite matrix $\Gamma$ has $\|\Gamma\|_{\rm op}>R(x)$, a top unit eigenvector $u$ gives $u^T\Gamma u=\|\Gamma\|_{\rm op}> (u^Tx_i)^2$ for every $i$, so the empirical upper weak tail is zero and the dense depth is zero. In the global block-sparse class, write $\Gamma$ as its symmetric block on some support $S$, $|S|\le s$, and its diagonal complement. The largest eigenvalue is attained either by a unit eigenvector in that block or by a coordinate vector in the complement; choose the former in a tie when the block is nonempty. Hence a norm-attaining vector has support of size at most $s$ or one, extends to a coordinate set of size $2s$, and belongs to $U_s$. The same strict inequality makes the sparse depth zero. This argument selects one appropriate eigenvector and does not claim every eigenvector is supported in a small block.

For $0\le j\le n$ and any fixed closed cube $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $H_{j,Q}:=\{x:\exists\Gamma\in K\cap Q,\ D(x,\Gamma)\ge j/n\}$. This is closed. Indeed its defining superlevel set is closed by step 1.1, and $K\cap Q$ is compact. If $x_0\notin H_{j,Q}$, product-open rectangles in the complement of that superlevel set cover $\{x_0\}\times(K\cap Q)$. Finitely many matrix-coordinate neighborhoods cover $K\cap Q$; intersect their sample-coordinate neighborhoods to obtain a neighborhood of $x_0$ outside $H_{j,Q}$. The empty $K\cap Q$ case gives the empty hit set. The same argument with $Q=\mathbb R^d$ gives a closed set $H_j:=\{x:\max_KD(x,\cdot)\ge j/n\}$.

Set $H_{n+1}=\varnothing$ and $E_j=H_j\setminus H_{j+1}$ for $0\le j\le n$. These are Borel by [F4] and partition $E$, since the maximum exists by [F2] and takes a value in the finite grid by step 1.1. On $E_j$, the argmax fiber is $A(x)=\{\Gamma\in K:D(x,\Gamma)\ge j/n\}$, so $A(x)$ hits a fixed closed cube $Q$ exactly when $x\in H_{j,Q}$.

Take a fixed closed cube $Q_0$ containing $K$; the entry bound in the proof of [F2] permits $Q_0=[-c,c]^d$. Repeatedly bisect each coordinate interval into two closed halves, ordering the $2^d$ child cubes lexicographically. On $E_j$, starting from $Q_0$, retain the first child cube $Q$ with $x\in H_{j,Q}$. A child exists because the children cover their parent and the parent meets $A(x)$. Inductively every selected-cube event is Borel: if $B$ is the event selecting a parent with ordered children $Q_1,\ldots,Q_{2^d}$, the event selecting $Q_r$ is $B\cap H_{j,Q_r}\setminus\bigcup_{\ell<r}H_{j,Q_\ell}$. Each level has finitely many cubes, so its selected center $a_m(x)$ is a finite-valued Borel map. The first-child rule remains unambiguous at overlapping cube boundaries.

For fixed $x$, the sets $A(x)\cap Q_m(x)$ are nested nonempty compact sets and the cubes have diameter $2c\sqrt d\,2^{-m}\to0$. Their intersection is nonempty: otherwise their complements would cover the first compact set, and a finite subcover would contradict a later set's nonemptiness. The intersection has at most one point because its diameter is zero; denote the point by $\widehat\Gamma_c(x)$. Since both it and $a_m(x)$ lie in $Q_m(x)$, $\|a_m(x)-\widehat\Gamma_c(x)\|_2$ is at most the cube diameter and tends to zero. Thus each coordinate of $\widehat\Gamma_c$ is Borel by [F5], and the matrix-valued map is Borel by [F6]. It belongs to $A(x)$ for every sample. Taking $c=\beta M$ proves both original bounded-class selection claims.

The continuous function $R$ has a Borel integer majorant $k(x)=1+\lfloor R(x)\rfloor$, with $\{k=\ell\}=\{\ell-1\le R<\ell\}$ for $\ell\ge1$. On that stratum, step 1.2 shows that every admissible matrix outside the fixed cap $\ell$ has depth zero. The maximum over the cap is nonnegative, so any cap maximizer is a global maximizer. Apply the explicit construction of steps 1.1–5.1 with $c=\ell$ for each integer $\ell\ge1$ and paste those Borel maps on the Borel strata $\{k=\ell\}$. For any open set of matrices, the preimage under this pasted map is the countable union, over $\ell\ge1$, of the Borel stratum $\{k=\ell\}$ intersected with the preimage under its fixed-cap Borel selector; hence the pasted map is Borel. This yields a Borel global maximizer in each class. Global argmax fibers need not be compact when the maximal depth is zero; only their compact capped subfibers are used. Division by the fixed $\beta>0$ preserves coordinatewise Borel measurability, proving the covariance-output claim for bounded and global selectors.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

For a bounded function continuous on the closed strip and holomorphic inside, the vertical-line supremum is log-convex.

Precisely, let $S=\{z:0\le\operatorname{Re}z\le1\}$, let $f:S\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and continuous and holomorphic on the open strip, and define
$$M(x):=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}|f(x+iy)|\qquad(0\le x\le1).$$
Then, for $0<\theta<1$,
$$M(\theta)\le M(0)^{1-\theta}M(1)^\theta.$$
More generally, for $0\le x_0<x_1\le1$ and $0<t<1$,
$$M((1-t)x_0+tx_1)\le M(x_0)^{1-t}M(x_1)^t.$$
Both displayed inequalities are asserted only for strictly interior parameters, $0<\theta<1$ and $0<t<1$, so both exponents are strictly positive and the positive-exponent convention $0^s=0$ applies when a boundary supremum is zero ([[def-real-power]]); the excluded endpoint expressions $M(0)^0$ and $M(1)^0$ would be the undefined $0^0$ when that supremum vanishes.

derivations.claim: We first record two elementary trace estimates. If $A=U\operatorname{diag}(a_j)V^*$ is a singular value decomposition, cyclically expanding the finite diagonal sum gives $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\sum_j a_j\langle V^*BUe_j,e_j\rangle$, so $|\operatorname{tr}(AB)|\le\|A\|_1\|B\|_{\rm op}$. Also $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}$, so scalar Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\operatorname{tr}(AB)|\le\|A\|_2\|B\|_2$, since $\|A\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^*A)=\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2$ by the singular value decomposition. These arguments also prove the trace cyclicity used here by interchanging two finite sums.

Set $F(z)=\exp(zH/2)\exp(zK/2)$ and $M=\|\exp(H/2)\exp(K/2)\|_2>0$. The function $F$ is entrywise entire and uniformly bounded on the closed strip: for $z=x+iy$ each exponential is the product of a bounded positive real exponential with a unitary imaginary exponential of the same Hermitian matrix. On the line $x=0$, $\|F(iy)\|_{\rm op}=1$. On $x=1$, the identity $F(1+iy)=\exp(iyH/2)\exp(H/2)\exp(K/2)\exp(iyK/2)$ and unitary invariance give $\|F(1+iy)\|_2=M$.

We need a finite eigenvalue comparison only for a diagonalizable invertible matrix $A$. Order its eigenvalue moduli and its singular values decreasingly. For $1\le k\le p$, the $k$th exterior space has the orthonormal wedge basis $e_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{j_k}$, $j_1<\cdots<j_k$, and its induced map sends a wedge to the wedge of the images. This defines the finite matrix $\bigwedge^k A$ directly by multilinearity and alternation. The singular value decomposition makes its norm $\prod_{j=1}^k s_j(A)$: wedges of the two singular-vector orthonormal bases give diagonal coefficients consisting of all $k$-fold singular-value products. Wedges of the first $k$ independent eigenvectors are nonzero eigenvectors with eigenvalue $\prod_{j=1}^k\lambda_j(A)$; nonvanishing follows by expanding independent vectors in a basis and noting that some $k$-minor is nonzero. The norm bounds the modulus of an eigenvalue, proving $\prod_{j=1}^k|\lambda_j(A)|\le\prod_{j=1}^k s_j(A)$. This uses only finite bases and finite determinants.

Fix $0<s<1$, put $q=2/s$ and $q'=2/(2-s)$, and choose a singular value decomposition $F(s)=U\operatorname{diag}(a_j)V^*$. All $a_j$ are positive because $F(s)$ is invertible. Set $N=(\sum_j a_j^q)^{1/q}>0$ and $b_j=(a_j/N)^{q-1}$, so $\sum_j b_j^{q'}=1$. Define $G(z)=V\operatorname{diag}(\exp(q'(1-z/2)\log b_j))U^*$ and $g(z)=\operatorname{tr}(G(z)F(z))$. These functions are continuous and bounded on the closed strip and holomorphic inside: their entries are finite sums of entire exponentials and their moduli are bounded uniformly in the imaginary coordinate. On its left boundary $\|G(iy)\|_1=\sum_j b_j^{q'}=1$, and on its right boundary $\|G(1+iy)\|_2=(\sum_j b_j^{q'})^{1/2}=1$. The two trace estimates of step 1.1 therefore bound $|g|$ by $1$ and $M$ on the respective boundaries. Since $q'(1-s/2)=1$, one has $g(s)=\sum_j a_jb_j=N$. Applying [F3] yields $\|F(s)\|_{2/s}\le M^s$.

Put $x_j=\log|\lambda_j(A)|$ and $y_j=\log s_j(A)$ in decreasing order. Step 1.3 gives $\sum_{j=1}^k x_j\le\sum_{j=1}^k y_j$ for every $k$. For any real $u$, the positive terms form an initial segment, so $\sum_j(x_j-u)_+=\max_{0\le k\le p}(\sum_{j=1}^k x_j-ku)\le\sum_j(y_j-u)_+$. For every $c>0$, multiply by $c^2e^{cu}$ and integrate: $c^2\int_{-\infty}^x(x-u)e^{cu}\,du=e^{cx}$, as follows by evaluating the elementary exponential primitive at finite lower limits and sending that limit to $-\infty$. The finite sums can be integrated termwise and all integrands are nonnegative, giving $\sum_j|\lambda_j(A)|^c\le\sum_j s_j(A)^c$.

For each integer $n\ge2$, let $A_n=F(1/n)$. It is similar to the positive definite matrix $\exp(K/4n)\exp(H/2n)\exp(K/4n)$, since conjugating $A_n$ by $\exp(K/4n)$ gives that matrix. Thus [F2] makes $A_n$ diagonalizable with positive eigenvalues. Apply step 2.2 with $c=2n$ and step 2.1 with $s=1/n$ to obtain $\operatorname{tr}(A_n^{2n})\le\sum_j s_j(A_n)^{2n}=\|A_n\|_{2n}^{2n}\le M^2$.

The exponential series gives $A_n=I+(H+K)/(2n)+O(n^{-2})$ and $B_n:=\exp((H+K)/(2n))=I+(H+K)/(2n)+O(n^{-2})$ in operator norm, where the constants depend only on the fixed matrices. Also $\|A_n\|,\|B_n\|\le e^{c/n}$ for one fixed $c$. The telescoping identity $A^N-B^N=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}A^j(A-B)B^{N-1-j}$, valid by cancellation without commutativity, gives $\|A_n^{2n}-B_n^{2n}\|=O(n^{-1})$. The addition law for exponential series of scalar multiples of one matrix gives $B_n^{2n}=\exp(H+K)$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}\exp(H+K)=\lim_n\operatorname{tr}(A_n^{2n})\le M^2=\operatorname{tr}(\exp(H)\exp(K))$, using $|\operatorname{tr}C|\le p\|C\|_{\rm op}$ and cyclicity to evaluate the Hilbert–Schmidt square $M^2$. This is the claimed inequality.

$$\operatorname{tr}\exp(H+K)\le\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\exp(H)\exp(K)\bigr).$$
Here $\exp(A)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}A^j/j!$ is the norm-convergent finite-matrix exponential series. No commutativity assumption is imposed.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $0<s<3/R$. If $|x|\le R$ and $k\ge2$ is an integer, then $x^k\le R^{k-2}x^2$, including odd $k$ and negative $x$. Applying the spectral calculus and taking expectations gives $\mathbb E B_i^k\preceq R^{k-2}\mathbb E B_i^2$. Since $k!\ge2\cdot3^{k-2}$ for every $k\ge2$ (start at $k=2$ and multiply by $k+1\ge3$), the exponential series and $\mathbb EB_i=0$ yield $\mathbb E\exp(sB_i)\preceq I+g(s)\mathbb EB_i^2\preceq e^{g(s)v}I$, where $g(s)=s^2/[2(1-sR/3)]$. The first inequality is the sum of the convergent geometric majorant $\sum_{k\ge2}s^kR^{k-2}/k!\le g(s)$, and the second uses $0\preceq\mathbb EB_i^2\preceq vI$ and the scalar inequality $1+a\le e^a$. Termwise expectation is justified by the uniform norm majorant $\sum_k(sR)^k/k!$.

Let $Y_j=\sum_{i=1}^jB_i$, with $Y_0=0$. For each fixed value of $Y_{j-1}$, [F2] and integration over the independent $B_j$ give $\mathbb E_{B_j}\operatorname{tr}\exp(sY_{j-1}+sB_j)\le\operatorname{tr}(\exp(sY_{j-1})\mathbb E\exp(sB_j))\le e^{g(s)v}\operatorname{tr}\exp(sY_{j-1})$. The last implication follows because $P\succeq0$ and $Q\preceq cI$ imply $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)\le c\operatorname{tr}P$: diagonalize $P$ and sum its nonnegative eigenvalues times the bounded diagonal quadratic forms of $Q$. Successive integration using [F3] and iteration from $\operatorname{tr}I=q$ prove $\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}\exp(sY)\le qe^{mg(s)v}$.

By [F1], $\operatorname{tr}\exp(sY)\ge\exp(s\lambda_{\max}(Y))$. Markov's inequality [F4] and step 2.1 therefore give $\mathbb P\{\lambda_{\max}(Y)\ge u\}\le q\exp(-su+mg(s)v)$ for every $u>0$ and $0<s<3/R$. If $v>0$, choose $s=u/(mv+Ru/3)$, which belongs to that interval. Substitution gives $-su+mg(s)v=-u^2/[2(mv+Ru/3)]$, proving the stated tail bound. The same fixed-parameter bound with $>$ in place of $\ge$ will also be used below.

For $b>0$ set $u=\sqrt{2mvb}+2Rb/3$. Expanding its square shows $u^2\ge2b(mv+Ru/3)$: with $a=\sqrt{2mvb}$ and $c=2Rb/3$, the two sides are respectively $a^2+2ac+c^2$ and $a^2+ac+c^2$. Thus step 3.1 bounds the one-sided failure by $qe^{-b}$. Applying the same argument to $-B_i$ and taking the union of the two failures bounds the norm failure by $2qe^{-b}$, since the norm of a Hermitian matrix is the larger of its maximum eigenvalue and the maximum eigenvalue of its negative.

Finally, if $v=0$, then for each coordinate vector $e_j$, $\mathbb E\|B_i e_j\|_2^2=e_j^*(\mathbb EB_i^2)e_j=0$. A nonnegative random variable with zero expectation vanishes almost surely: otherwise one of the events where it exceeds $1/n$ would have positive probability and positive contribution to the expectation. Intersecting the finitely many full-probability coordinate events gives $B_i=0$ almost surely; a further finite intersection covers all $i$. The trace mgf is then $q$ and both strict positive-threshold events are empty. This covers the remaining case and completes all conclusions.

Let $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ be independent centered random Hermitian $q\times q$ matrices, $q,m\ge1$. Suppose $R>0$, $v\ge0$, and
$$\|B_i\|_{\rm op}\le R\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad\|\mathbb E B_i^2\|_{\rm op}\le v\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Writing $Y=\sum_{i=1}^m B_i$, for $0<s<3/R$ one has
$$\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}\exp(sY)\le q\exp\left(\frac{ms^2v}{2(1-sR/3)}\right).$$
Consequently, for $u>0$ when $v>0$,
$$\mathbb P\{\lambda_{\max}(Y)\ge u\}\le q\exp\left(-\frac{u^2}{2(mv+Ru/3)}\right).$$
For every $b>0$, the following convenient forms also hold:
$$\mathbb P\left\{\lambda_{\max}(Y)>\sqrt{2mvb}+\frac{2Rb}{3}\right\}\le qe^{-b},\qquad\mathbb P\left\{\|Y\|_{\rm op}>\sqrt{2mvb}+\frac{2Rb}{3}\right\}\le2qe^{-b}.$$
If $v=0$, all $B_i$ and $Y$ vanish almost surely, so the displayed positive-threshold conclusions remain valid.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

derivations.claim: Put $A=ZZ^T$ and $A_\theta=w(Z)ZZ^T$. The weight is a Borel function, including its declared value at zero, so all transformations used here preserve the independence of the samples by [F3]. The rank-one spectral calculus gives $0\preceq A_\theta\preceq RI$ and $A_\theta^2\preceq A^2$. For a scalar $x\ge0$, $(x-R)_+\le x^2/(4R)$: the inequality is immediate for $x\le R$, and for $x\ge R$ it is equivalent to $(x-2R)^2\ge0$. Applying it to the eigenvalues of $A$ proves $0\preceq A-A_\theta\preceq\theta A^2/4$. Therefore $0\preceq\Sigma-\mathbb E A_\theta\preceq\theta\mathbb EA^2/4$ and $\|\Sigma-\mathbb E A_\theta\|_{\rm op}\le\theta\sigma_0^2/4$. Nonzero covariance also implies $\sigma_0>0$: a positive variance in some unit direction forces $\mathbb E[\|Z\|^2\langle Z,v\rangle^2]\ge\mathbb E\langle Z,v\rangle^4>0$. Thus the displayed thresholds are well-defined.

Put $Y=w(Z)Z$. Its norm is at most $1/\sqrt\theta$: for $\|Z\|\le\sqrt R$ use $\|Y\|\le\sqrt R$, and otherwise use $\|Y\|=R/\|Z\|\le\sqrt R$. Since $\mathbb EZ=0$, $\mathbb EY=-\mathbb E[(1-w(Z))Z]$. For a unit vector $v$, apply [F3] to $U=\|Z\|\langle Z,v\rangle$ and $W=(1-w(Z))/\|Z\|$, assigning $W=0$ at zero. Then $\mathbb EU^2\le\sigma_0^2$ by matrix variance, and $W^2\le\theta$ pointwise: it vanishes on $\|Z\|^2\le R$, and elsewhere is at most $1/\|Z\|^2\le1/R$. Thus $|\langle\mathbb EY,v\rangle|\le\sigma_0\sqrt\theta$. Taking the Euclidean dual supremum proves $\|\mathbb EY\|\le\sigma_0\sqrt\theta$.

Set $B_i=A_{\theta,i}-\mathbb E A_\theta$. Since both matrices subtracted lie between $0$ and $RI$, $-RI\preceq B_i\preceq RI$, whence $\|B_i\|_{\rm op}\le R$. Expanding the square and taking expectations, without any commutativity requirement, gives $\mathbb E B_i^2=\mathbb EA_\theta^2-(\mathbb EA_\theta)^2\preceq\mathbb EA^2$. The left side is positive semidefinite; hence its norm is at most $\sigma_0^2$. The matrices $B_i$ are independent and centered.

For a vector $y\in\mathbb R^p$ define its symmetric dilation $D(y)=\begin{pmatrix}0&y^T\\y&0\end{pmatrix}$ of size $p+1$. Its square is $\operatorname{diag}(\|y\|_2^2,yy^T)$; its nonzero eigenvalues when $y\ne0$ are $\|y\|_2$ and $-\|y\|_2$, as is checked on the span of $(1,0)$ and $(0,y/\|y\|)$. It vanishes on the orthogonal complement, so $\lambda_{\max}(D(y))=\|D(y)\|_{\rm op}=\|y\|_2$, also at zero. For $C_i=D(Y_i-\mathbb EY)$, step 1.2 gives $\|C_i\|\le2/\sqrt\theta$. The square identity gives $\mathbb E C_i^2=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbb E\|Y-\mathbb EY\|^2,\mathbb E[(Y-\mathbb EY)(Y-\mathbb EY)^T])$. Its norm is at most $\mathbb E\|Y-\mathbb EY\|^2\le\mathbb E\|Y\|^2\le\mathbb E\|Z\|^2=T$; for the lower block, test a unit vector and bound its squared scalar projection by the squared norm. The $C_i$ are independent centered symmetric matrices.

Let $b=\beta+\log2$ and use [F2] with the fixed Chernoff parameter $s=\theta$; it is admissible since $\theta R=1<3$. Its exponent bound is $3m\theta^2\sigma_0^2/4$. Consequently, for $u=3m\theta\sigma_0^2/4+b/\theta$, the one-sided failure is at most $pe^{-b}$; apply the same statement to $-B_i$ and take a union to obtain $\mathbb P\{\|S-\mathbb EA_\theta\|_{\rm op}>3\theta\sigma_0^2/4+b/(m\theta)\}\le2pe^{-b}=pe^{-\beta}$. Adding the bias from step 1.1 and using $\sigma_0\le\sigma$ yields $\theta\sigma_0^2+b/(m\theta)\le(2+(\log2)/\beta)\sigma\sqrt t$. Define $E_S$ by this bound. Finally $\log2<7/10$ since the first four nonnegative terms of $e^{7/10}$ sum to $1+7/10+49/200+343/6000>2$; since $\beta>1$, the claimed strict bound by $27/10$ follows.

For the alternative radius, apply the two-sided explicit form in [F2] to the same $B_i$, now with confidence parameter $\beta$. After division by $m$ its radius is $\sqrt{2\sigma_0^2\beta/m}+2R\beta/(3m)$. Adding the bias $\theta\sigma_0^2/4$ and substituting $R=1/\theta$, $\theta=\sqrt t/\sigma$, and $\sigma_0\le\sigma$, gives the displayed radius $(\sqrt2+2/3+1/4)\sigma\sqrt t$ with failure at most $2pe^{-\beta}$.

Apply the one-sided explicit Bernstein bound [F2] to $C_i$ with dimension $p+1$, bound $R_0=2/\sqrt\theta$, variance bound $v=T$ and confidence $b=\beta+\log2$. Since $\lambda_{\max}(\sum_i C_i)=\|\sum_i(Y_i-\mathbb EY)\|$, division by $m$ gives $\|V-\mathbb EY\|\le\sqrt{2Tb/m}+4b/(3m\sqrt\theta)$ outside probability $(p+1)e^{-b}=(p+1)e^{-\beta}/2$. Because $\log2<1<\beta$, one has $b<2\beta$, and the radius is at most $2\sqrt{Tt}+8t/(3\sqrt\theta)$. Adding step 1.2 proves the stated vector bound and defines $E_V$. The two events were obtained from the original independent observations without conditioning on any other statistic. Together with steps 3.1 and 3.2 this proves every asserted conclusion.

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $m_1,\ldots,m_k\in H$, and let $m$ minimize $F(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$. For $0<a<1/2$ and $r>0$, put
$$
C_a=\frac{1-a}{\sqrt{1-2a}}.
$$
If $z\in H$ satisfies $\|m-z\|>C_a r$, then more than $ak$ of the points $m_j$ satisfy $\|m_j-z\|>r$.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $n\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le n$ be an integer. Given $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in H^n$, put $q=\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ and $r=n-kq$. Form consecutive blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ in index order, with $|B_j|=q+1$ for $j\le r$ and $|B_j|=q$ for $j>r$. Compute the block means $m_j=|B_j|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}x_i$. Return the unique minimum-norm point of
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in H}\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|.
$$

The objective minimizers are called geometric medians of the block means. The minimum-norm rule makes the output single-valued. Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

Fix a separable real Hilbert space $H$ and an integer $k\ge1$. The rule in [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] defines a single-valued Borel map $H^k\to H$: for every tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)$ the function $F_m(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$ has a nonempty closed convex minimizer set, and that set has a unique point of minimum norm. The choice-free Borel construction below does not use weak compactness or reflexivity. Countable Choice is used only for the published Hilbert projection supplier that identifies the minimum-norm point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Suppose $T>0$, put $a=7/18$, $q=1/10$, $b=\lfloor m/k\rfloor$, and $r=\sqrt{T/(qb)}$. For a block of size $b_j$, expand $E\|b_j^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}(X_i-\mu)\|_2^2$: diagonal terms sum to $b_jT$ by [F2], and each cross term has expectation zero by [F3], because it is integrable by [F4] and the centered factors are independent. Thus $E\|M_j-\mu\|_2^2=T/b_j\le T/b$. Markov [F4] gives $P(\|M_j-\mu\|_2>r)\le q$. Grouping and measurable images in [F3] make the bad-block indicators independent.

Let $W$ be the number of bad blocks. For any $\lambda>0$, independence gives $E e^{\lambda W}\le(1-q+qe^\lambda)^k$: each Bernoulli factor is $1+P(\text{bad})(e^\lambda-1)\le1+q(e^\lambda-1)$, and [F3, F6] factor the product. Since $a>q$, choose $\lambda=\log(a(1-q)/(q(1-a)))>0$.
